summary: This informational memo describes how a network access server sends accounting information to a shared accounting server, as a companion to RADIUS. It was replaced by RFC 2866.

plainLanguage.summary: A meter that records how long each guest stays, reported to a central record book.

subtitle: Tracking network access server usage with a central accounting server.

tldr.problem: Network access servers needed a way to track and report how users were accessing the network, such as connection time, data transferred, and when sessions ended.
tldr.mechanism: RADIUS Accounting extends the RADIUS protocol with accounting request and response packets that the NAS sends to an accounting server, containing details about sessions like duration, data sent and received, and how the session ended.
tldr.outcome: This allowed network providers to bill users accurately and track resource usage centrally, replacing the need for local accounting mechanisms on each NAS.

today: RFC 2139 was declared obsolete in 2000 when RFC 2866 was issued as the standard RADIUS Accounting specification. RFC 2866 is itself now updated by RFC 9293.

sections.title: What RADIUS Accounting Does
sections.content:
RFC 2139 describes RADIUS Accounting, a protocol that lets a Network Access Server (NAS) report details about user sessions to a central accounting server. A NAS is a device that manages connections from dial-in users, such as a modem pool for internet service providers.

When a user connects, the NAS sends an accounting start packet. When the user disconnects, it sends a stop packet with statistics like how long the session lasted, how much data they transferred, and why the connection ended. The accounting server logs this information and sends back acknowledgements.

The protocol uses a client-server model where the NAS is the client and the accounting server is the server. They share a secret value for authentication, but the secret is never sent over the network.
sections.plainLanguage: When a guest arrives, the front desk calls the central office to log the check-in time. When they leave, it calls again to log how long they stayed and if they used the gym or pool.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
The accounting flow is simple. When the NAS delivers service to a user, it sends an Accounting-Request packet with status type Start, describing the service and the user receiving it. The accounting server responds with an Accounting-Response acknowledging receipt.

When the service ends, the NAS sends another Accounting-Request with status type Stop, including statistics like elapsed time, bytes transferred in and out, and the reason the session ended (such as user request, idle timeout, or admin reset). Again, the server acknowledges.

The NAS should retry sending requests if it does not receive an acknowledgement, and can forward to an alternate server if the primary is unreachable. The accounting server must not send an acknowledgement if it fails to record the packet, so the NAS knows to retry.
sections.plainLanguage: The meter sends two messages: one when the guest arrives and one when they leave, with a count of how much they used. Each time, the meter waits for a signal back saying the office got the message.

sections.title: Message Structure
sections.content:
Every RADIUS Accounting message is a single UDP packet sent to port 1813. (Earlier deployments used port 1646 by mistake, but 1813 is the official port.) The packet contains a 20-byte header followed by optional attributes.

The header includes a Code field (one byte) identifying the message type: code 4 for Accounting-Request and code 5 for Accounting-Response. The Identifier field (one byte) matches requests with replies. The Length field (two bytes) states the total packet size, from 20 bytes minimum to 4096 maximum. The Authenticator field (16 bytes) is an MD5 checksum that proves the message is authentic using the shared secret.

For a Request, the authenticator is computed as an MD5 hash of the code, identifier, length, 16 zero octets, the request attributes, and the shared secret concatenated together. For a Response, it is computed from the response code, identifier, length, the original request's authenticator, response attributes if any, and the shared secret.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message has a label saying if it is the start or the stop, a number matching it to the other message, the length so you know where it ends, and a secret stamp to prove nobody changed it on the way.

sections.title: Accounting Attributes
sections.content:
The packet's attributes are variable-length fields carrying specific accounting data. The protocol defines 12 accounting-specific attributes, and can also include general RADIUS attributes from the main protocol (except User-Password, CHAP-Password, Reply-Message, and State, which must not appear in accounting).

Acct-Status-Type (type 40) marks whether this is a Start, Stop, Accounting-On (server startup), or Accounting-Off (server shutdown) event. Acct-Session-Id (type 44) is a unique string tying a user's start and stop records together, often an 8-digit hexadecimal number. Acct-Session-Time (type 46) counts seconds the user received service; it appears only in Stop records.

Acct-Input-Octets (type 42) and Acct-Output-Octets (type 43) record bytes received from and sent to the port, appearing only in Stop records. Acct-Input-Packets (type 47) and Acct-Output-Packets (type 48) count packets. Acct-Terminate-Cause (type 49) explains why the session ended, using codes like 1 for user request, 4 for idle timeout, or 11 for NAS reboot.

Acct-Delay-Time (type 41) tells the server how many seconds the NAS was trying to send this record, helping compute the real time of the event. Acct-Multi-Session-Id (type 50) and Acct-Link-Count (type 51) support multilink sessions, where a single user session uses multiple ports or lines.
sections.plainLanguage: The message body contains facts about the visit: when it started or stopped, how long it lasted, how much stuff they downloaded or uploaded, and why they left.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
RADIUS Accounting security rests on the shared secret. The NAS and accounting server are configured with the same secret, never transmitted over the network. The Authenticator field in every message is an MD5 hash computed using this secret, so the server can verify the message came from the correct NAS and was not altered in transit.

Every Accounting-Request must contain either a NAS-IP-Address or NAS-Identifier attribute so the server knows which NAS sent it. An Accounting-Request must not include User-Password or CHAP-Password attributes, because the NAS has already authenticated the user via a separate RADIUS Access request and does not need to send passwords in the accounting stream.

The protocol assumes the network path between NAS and server is reasonably trusted. If an attacker intercepts a message, they cannot forge a reply without the shared secret. However, they could replay an old message, so implementations should guard against this by retiring old identifiers or checking timestamps with Acct-Delay-Time.
sections.plainLanguage: The front desk and the office use a secret password both know, so they can prove to each other that each message is real and nobody snooped it on the way.

fields.name: Code
fields.desc: Packet type: 4 for Accounting-Request, 5 for Accounting-Response.

fields.name: Identifier
fields.desc: Matches related request and response packets.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total packet size including header and attributes, 20 to 4096 bytes.

fields.name: Authenticator
fields.desc: 16-byte MD5 hash for authentication using the shared secret.
